Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that Letby had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told. Continue reading...

articles.title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
articles.description: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. articles.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
articles.description: He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original ‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.” Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats. articles.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
articles.description: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs. Continue reading...

articles.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
articles.description: After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI . But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You could argue this show cheats by cutting out that medieval context of prayer and faith. It’s also a great way for the gallery to show off that it owns three of his greatest portraits. Yet the result makes you see the utterly strange way he collects his slightly miniaturised people like flies in amber. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘We want our story to be told’: inside a shocking 36-year fight for justice in Baltimore
articles.description: A staggering case of injustice is explored in the galling HBO documentary When a Witness Recants. The three subjects and producer Ta-Nehisi Coates explain how it unfolded For most of his life, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates would occasionally think of a chilling episode from his childhood in West Baltimore: almost exactly 43 years ago, on 18 November 1983, a 14-year-old boy named DeWitt Duckett was shot and killed in a hallway of Harlem Park junior high school in the middle of the afternoon, by an older teenager who stole his blue satin Georgetown jacket. Coates was only eight years old at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. The sensational event – the first time a kid was killed inside a Baltimore public school, according to wall-to-wall local press – was a rupture in his child’s view of the world. “It was first time I had the sense that, oh, actually, I exist in a very dangerous world,” he told the Guardian. “And then you cut to the TV and it’s clear the rest of America is not existing in that dangerous world. The dangerous world is only for you and people who look like you.” Coates always assumed that the three teenage boys arrested and convicted for the murder were the right guys, and the episode faded into one of those strange imprints from the past, a blurry but foundational event. articles.description: As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms. The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxiety and depression, impeding their ability to work, they are often castigated as feckless snowflakes. It is easier to do this than admit that we have failed a generation, and that this is the predictable consequence of political decisions. articles.description: Scientific discoveries are effortlessly explained in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. articles.title: A moment that changed me: the tomato pasta that became an obsession – and helped me lead a better life
articles.description: At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. I spent four days with his lovely family, in the rolling verdant hills, with fireflies and fallow deer keeping us company, drinking vernaccia and talking of books and art and poetry. But none of that matters, not even a bit. All that matters is a single plate of tomato pasta from Nuova Trattoria Albana , in Mazzolla, west of Siena. This pasta might have seemed, to the untrained palate, like any other pasta. But it changed everything for me. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The aesthetics in my family were so high, I felt ugly’: Charlotte Gainsbourg on extremism, abortion and her mother, Jane Birkin
articles.description: In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier While she was making the film Women on Trial , about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France. The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.” Continue reading...

articles.description: Updates on the final ODI in the series at Bellerive Oval Play start time in Hobart is 2.30pm AEDT/3.30am BST Any thoughts? Get in touch with an email We are indeed very, very proud the culture that this team has built the past eight years. Our players our leaders, our coaches deserve enormous credit for that. In particular Pat and Andrew who continue to lead this team with distinction. But we recognise the pain and the hurt that events surrounding sandpaper have caused. The game is genuinely hurting the moment. It’s not good for anyone. We need to find a path through, we need some time to heal. As of this process, and so all parties who wish to can tell their version of events we have set up now an independent forum, a chance to give everyone a voice in an independent a safe setting. It’s not investigation. It’s not to produce a sanction. No one is forced to participate. It is entirely up to each individual. It’s important to remember we’re talking about events that happened eight a half years ago. And I hope everyone will respect this process the players be afforded the space to at their best at what is a very important time and period for the game. CA CEO Todd Greenberg is ready to speak … For the past week we’ve had several different and conflicting accounts of what occurred in Cape Town in 2018. And it’s an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time the game and for who was involved. Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. There were stiff boxy pleated skirts and tube skirts painted with swirls, and dainty embellished skirts with a layer of gauze on top, like a petticoat worn on the outside. Continue reading...

articles.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
articles.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a lab coat and examine brain regions and neurochemicals, but studying the mechanics, he says, doesn’t damp down the mysteries of consciousness. “For me, actually, I’ve become more spiritual and interested in the world of mystery and, I want to say supernatural, but dimensions that are intangible, by studying something like sleep paralysis.” Continue reading...

articles.title: "Birds of War": New Film Tells a Story of Love and Journalism from Syria to Lebanon
articles.description: We speak with Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak, filmmakers and subjects of the new documentary Birds of War , which tells their epic love story through years of upheaval in the Middle East. Boulos, a London-based Lebanese journalist working for the BBC , and Habak, a Syrian activist and cameraman, first connected while covering the Syrian civil war and stayed in touch through years of war, revolution and exile, forming a relationship that is chronicled in the documentary by drawing on 13 years of their personal videos, voice notes and other correspondence. The film also examines the unequal relationship between international news organizations and local journalists whose work they rely on, the fraught political history between Syria and Lebanon, and how Boulos and Habak’s personal connection overcame those divisions. “Without our journalistic relationship, [we] would have never been together. I would have never opened my heart to somebody like him,” says Boulos. “We can be any race, any gender, any religion, any background, but at the same time we’re all humans.” Birds of War premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Documentary Special Jury Award for Journalistic Impact.

articles.title: Meet David Morales: Providence Voters Elect Democratic Socialist Mayor, Approve Israel Divestment
articles.description: Voters in Providence, Rhode Island, approved a ballot measure last week that could result in the city divesting from Israel. The successful grassroots campaign makes Providence the first U.S. city to pass a binding divestment measure through a popular vote. The measure instructs the city to divest from countries and companies implicated in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The language does not mention Israel by name. We speak with one of the key backers of the divestment measure, Mayor-elect David Morales, a 28-year-old democratic socialist who made history on election night as the youngest mayor ever elected in Providence. “What we saw was our neighbors coming out in the thousands to demonstrate that we are ready for change,” Morales says, promising to enact his affordability-focused platform. “It’s the responsibility of local government to take action. And for that reason, we are seeing a rise in democratic socialism and the representation of democratic socialists all across the country.”

articles.title: "American Scoundrel": From Roy Cohn to Stephen Miller, "McCarthyism Lives On," Says Author Kai Bird
articles.description: We speak with historian Kai Bird about American Scoundrel , a new biography of the notorious political fixer Roy Cohn, who rose to fame as chief counsel to Joe McCarthy during the senator’s anti-communist campaign, served as a lawyer for the New York mob, and was an influential voice in Republican circles until his death from AIDS -related complications in 1986. His most impactful relationship, however, would prove to be with a young Donald Trump, whom he mentored in business and politics during the 1970s and ’80s. Facing political setbacks during his first term as president, Trump reportedly asked, “Where’s my Roy Cohn?” Bird, who co-authored American Scoundrel with his wife Susan Goldmark, says Trump may have found his Cohn in Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s mass deportation policies whom Trump just elevated to chief of staff. “It’s not really a surprise that, cornered and wounded by the recent election results, he reaches out and pulls up Stephen Miller, who’s very similar in his willingness to go on the offensive and never back down, and to say outrageous things to try to change the narrative,” says Bird.

articles.title: "The Earth Shook Last Night": Talarico Wins Senate, Hinojosa Becomes First Latina Governor in Texas
articles.description: Texas Democrats have shattered more than three decades of Republican dominance in the state, winning races for U.S. Senate, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and even railroad commissioner. They are also poised to possibly take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2003. The Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, lost his bid for a fourth term to Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa, who defeated him by nearly 700,000 votes. She will be Texas’s first Latina governor. And James Talarico will be the first Democrat to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate since 1993. “We’re celebrating these wonderful candidates who won office, and we’re also starting to think about what it means to hold power,” says Mike Siegel, a city council member from Austin, Texas, who founded Ground Game Texas, a statewide voter turnout organization. “We need to start thinking very quickly about how we will protect public education, how we will stop data centers and the encroachment of AI on our society, how we will protect public schools, how we stop collaboration with ICE .”

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed Becomes First Muslim Senator as Democrats Rout GOP Across the U.S. in Rebuke to Trump
articles.description: In a stunning repudiation of President Trump, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. Meanwhile, progressive Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican Congressmember Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat in Michigan with over 52% of the vote. El-Sayed campaigned on a platform of Medicare for All, tackling economic inequality and getting big money out of politics — as well as ending military aid to Israel. He is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. El-Sayed faced vitriolic, Islamaphobic attacks by top Republicans throughout the campaign. “Last night wasn’t just about Dr. Abdulrahman being a Muslim, winning and going to the United States Senate,” says Palestinian American organizer and author Linda Sarsour, who has been campaigning for El-Sayed. “It demonstrated that progressives can win in states like Michigan” and that “we can win on standing up for the human rights of the Palestinian people.”

articles.title: The Last Spy review – a riveting tale of CIA meddling, espionage gossip and Blue Nun wine
articles.description: Refugee Peter Sichel was known as ‘the Jewish James Bond’ after fleeing Germany and becoming an integral cold war-era spy. He died last year but, at 100-years-old, he told his remarkable story for this film Why, exactly, was Peter Sichel “the last spy”? It’s not something Katharina Otto-Bernstein’s documentary about the cold war-era CIA man clarifies. The “Jewish James Bond” – as a woman from his synagogue nicknames him – is a catchier moniker, although that’s not quite right either. If Sichel was once a swashbuckling secret agent, we don’t hear much about his escapades here. Instead, he seems closer to M: sitting behind a desk pulling strings while his agents risked life and limb sneaking around the German Democratic Republic. The Last Spy begins as a straightforward but riveting biography built around a long, candid interview with Sichel, who was 100 at the time of filming (he died last year at 102). We hear about his childhood in Germany, which was initially privileged thanks to his great-grandfather’s lucrative wine business. Yet his mother was spooked early on by the rise of Hitler, and insisted the family relocate to France. When war did break out, all Germans were considered “enemy aliens” and sent to internment camps. Later, when the German army advanced, the Jews were allowed to make a run for it, pursued by warplanes. After hiding out near the Pyrenees, Sichel and his family escaped to New York in 1941 – only to find themselves living beside a Nazi-supporting neighbourhood on the Upper East side. Continue reading...

articles.title: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone
articles.description: He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report? It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone. What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security . Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
articles.description: This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate. Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work , he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit. articles.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
articles.description: Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year. “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis , ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation. articles.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
articles.description: The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over. Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. I never spoke about them to anyone. I experienced hallucinations in the form of severe perspective distortion (oversized bed and rooms) and full hallucinations/dream states, auditory hallucinations (screaming and loud thumping) and, of course, paralysis. I didn’t know at what point I was asleep or if I had woken and could easily slip back into a hypnagogic state. I only became aware of this state as an adult, having been referred to a psychiatrist on an unrelated matter. Continue reading...

articles.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.description: With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south. Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable
articles.description: The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments. There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. I was reminded of Shameless (the US version) as much as Steinbeck. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
articles.description: Royal Academy, London The modernist collector once ran a gallery in London – but from this confusing exhibition, it’s hard to tell what exactly was once in there Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky , Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy . How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful of captions list definitive instances. Does this imply that where not stated, they are included for illustrative purposes? This may be due to relevant works being difficult to obtain; for the segment representing Jean Cocteau’s exhibition in January 1938 we have one of his ink drawings for his 1937 play Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde, and another in reproduction only. articles.title: A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese
articles.description: Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side. Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food. Continue reading...

articles.description: Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that these physical media hold. Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic . “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.” Continue reading...

articles.title: I got scammed on Instagram – and it led to a truly disgusting dinner | Zoe Williams
articles.description: Intrigued by an unusual recipe for spinach tacos, I followed the instructions, but was left with a soggy, inedible mess. It turns out there are a lot of made-up meals out there I can’t tell you when my Instagram algorithm changed, from – this is embarrassing, but what the hell – buff guys trying to exercise and being interrupted by a Staffordshire bull terrier who wants to help them exercise, to cooking videos, but it has. I now get endless food content, following the same format: a millennial has 20 minutes to make dinner for his or her beloved (it’s very gender neutral), and launches into some unlikely techniques. He might shove a load of chicken into a cake tin, sprinkle mismatched spices all over, bake it, then slice it, as if it were a cake. Or she might cook tagliatelle in a pan of milk and salmon. This is not how it’s done, I think, as I watch all the way to the end, and then am astonished to be fed yet more weird food content. Drawn with an almost zombified lack of free will, I got the yen to try it for myself. What would happen if you boiled a white cabbage whole, then roasted it in honey and miso? Well, I can tell you: the cabbage is very soft on the outside, and still uncooked on the inside, and this is why cooks, since time began, have been slicing a cabbage before they try to cook it. A sliver of hope is the trio of doctors it profiles, individuals acting on their conscience. (The same can be said of director Poh Si Teng , who quit her job at ABC News and cashed in her savings to get the documentary off the ground.) It follows three American doctors who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital in southern Gaza in early 2025 – though one of the trio, Thaer Ahmad, an ER doctor of Palestinian heritage from Chicago, is refused entry the night before they enter Gaza. His colleagues, Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon, and Dr Mark Perlmutter, a Jewish-American orthopaedic surgeon, complete the mission. This is not the first time in Gaza for either of them. Before he leaves, Perlmutter packs antibiotics into a dozen or so little plastic bags dotted around his luggage; that way if he gets turned back at the border, he stands a chance of getting some of the life-saving medication through. articles.title: Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so
articles.description: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy unpicked Darwinian sexism to rewrite the story of evolution. Now, she’s turned her attention to the nature of fatherhood ‘Spit here, dear,” Sarah Blaffer Hrdy said to her husband, Dan, handing him a vial when he arrived in New York after the birth of the couple’s first grandchild. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones. It did, although it took a day longer. In her latest book, Father Time: A Natural History of Men and Babies , Hrdy records with justified pride that “this was the first time anyone had demonstrated a bump in oxytocin levels among doting grandparents”. articles.title: Rocky is Philadelphia’s founding myth – and 50 years later, we’re still telling it
articles.description: As Sylvester Stallone’s Oscar-winning drama celebrates its 50th anniversary, I Play Rocky helps to further turn the boxing hero into the stuff of legend The story behind the making of Rocky has always sounded uncannily like Rocky itself. An unknown with an improbable dream, a skeptical establishment and a refusal to accept the odds: Sylvester Stallone’s real-life struggle to crack the industry and bring his breakthrough film to the screen contained all the elements of the underdog story he sought to tell. Now, half a century later, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky has crafted those parallels into a crowd-pleasing yarn of its own. It’s an extraordinary afterlife for a modest boxing flick that became the highest-grossing film of 1976 on a $1m budget and won the Oscar for best picture over one of the most stacked fields in history. Yet its greatest achievement may be the durability of the story – dismissed then by the New York Times as a “sentimental little slum movie” and Gene Siskel as a “flatout schmaltzy saga” – that we’re still finding new ways to repurpose all these years later through six Rocky films, three Creed sequels, a Broadway musical , and too many documentaries, novelizations and video games to count. At some point long ago, a screenplay written in three and a half days and never envisioned as IP became something closer to contemporary folklore. Continue reading...

Newsom, a likely candidate for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, has endorsed the Santa Marta Process, a coalition of nations working to develop a global green energy transition. “The petrostates have made it abundantly clear: Under the current rules of consensus, they are never, ever going to allow COPs to succeed. articles.description: What will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? We speak to Kumi Naidoo, the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, which aims to reach a binding agreement for a global transition away from fossil fuels. Currently backed by over 25 countries from the Global South, the intergovernmental process began earlier this year in Santa Marta, Colombia. Meanwhile, at the United Nations, “for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels [in the outcome document]. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol,” says Naidoo. We discuss the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative’s goals, how the oil and gas industry drives global conflict, and the Trump administration’s glaring absence from international action on climate change.

articles.description: Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come. Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable. articles.title: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis
articles.description: The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele. The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me ). But after working with the food magazine Vittles on its inaugural London vegan guide , I have begun to challenge the “death of vegan dining” narrative that I had found myself perpetuating. And yes, a depressing number of my choices for the Vegan 99 closed while I was writing it; most recently, an omnivorous Malaysian restaurant with a walloping double-tofu laksa, which shut 24 hours before publication. But the process encouraged me to take a different viewpoint, instead focusing on the spots that had survived and the story they told. Isobel Lewis is a freelance culture and lifestyle journalist Continue reading...

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. So what happens next?
articles.description: The wait for the new Bond is over but that’s only the beginning – there are still small issues such as the script, title, setting, casting, branding and promotion … • Robert Pattinson announced as James Bond – news • Share your thoughts on the casting • Peter Bradshaw’s take • Pattinson’s journey to James Bond • Behind Bond’s bankability It’s official: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond . While never a certainty for the role, for those reading the runes inside the film industry, the announcement will have been a tiny bit anticlimactic. Ever since it emerged that the film’s producers appeared unsatisfied with their initial shortlist and called in Pattinson alongside Nicholas Hoult, it appeared that in this new era for Bond under Amazon MGM, the traditional Bond barrier against an established Hollywood leading man was no longer in place. And with no shade to Hoult, Pattinson’s record at delivering in major franchises – Twilight, The Batman, Dune – as well as his classy acting CV put him firmly in the driving seat. In another departure from traditional 007 practice, Amazon MGM announced the casting decision via posts on social media , rather than at a press call in a fancy London hotel, which is how the world officially found out about George Lazenby, Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan . Although this will have been thought through as a way to maximise audience engagement with the forthcoming film, it perhaps is a disappointment to Bond purists that a big show wasn’t staged, and it may be Amazon MGM’s next order of business to organise a fan-type convention – or even piggyback on the next big fanclub event, due in December – to present Pattinson to an adoring audience. articles.title: Heysel 85 review – rage-filled denunciation of the incompetence that fuelled a football disaster
articles.description: Teodora Ana Mihai and her passionately committed cast reconstruct the grim sequence of bad judgments that led to 39 fans dying Shame and rage are the keynotes of this immersive, viscerally powerful drama-thriller set amid the macabre tragedy of football’s 1985 European Cup final between Juventus and Liverpool in the crumbling Heysel stadium in Brussels. Crowd disorder before kickoff in a poorly maintained, badly policed venue resulted in the deaths of 39 fans. In this film, the roar of the crowd echoing overhead through the stadium’s claustrophobic tunnels is like the wailing of the damned, while the sport’s officer class flinch and panic as if at a wartime loss. Grimly, the match was allowed to go ahead, despite the fatalities; the authorities believed the game itself would restore order on a bread-and-circuses basis, and that abandoning the match would only cause greater violence and chaos. Heysel 85 is directed and co-written by Romanian-born and Belgian-based film-maker Teodora Ana Mihai; she is a former collaborator of Cristian Mungiu, though maybe the influence here is more Paul Greengrass. The film-makers have been criticised for fictionalising aspects: the players are depicted as not being aware that fans had died before they took to the field – they were in fact largely aware, although it may well be true that the slippery authorities sought to minimise the truth as much as they could. And the fictionalised mayor of Brussels, here named Marc Dumont (Josse De Pauw), has been criticised as an unfair drunken caricature of the actual mayor, Hervé Brouhon. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Brightness by Chad Harbach review – an ambitious sequel to The Art of Fielding
articles.description: Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place. Legend has it that Harbach laboured over The Art of Fielding for more than a decade. When it finally emerged, a feverish bidding war saw it sell for more than $650,000 (£431,000), a saga chronicled at length in Vanity Fair. Any follow-up to such a high-profile debut, let alone one 15 years in the making, was always going to be read against the original. The Brightness, set on the same campus and peopled by many of the same characters, all but demands direct comparison. Throw in the fact that Harbach’s first novel actually turns up inside its sequel, and we’re in metatextual heaven. In the four years of Westish time that have elapsed between the two books, Owen Dunne (baseball player in The Art of Fielding; groom-to-be here) has written and published, to great acclaim, a novel called – guess what! – The Art of Fielding. articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. articles.title: ‘His wife was horrified’: did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?
articles.description: He is the maestro of American melancholy. But in a new biography, the artist is called a ‘sadist’ and a ‘prize hog’ by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.” Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily diaries, almost 100 notebooks, reels of letters, and four ledger books documenting Edward’s works. articles.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
articles.description: It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing? In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate . In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble. Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m . Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files. articles.description: Ukraine again hits symbolic bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia; Kyiv’s heating and water disrupted as North and South bridges struck. What we know on day 1,728 Ukraine struck a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia for the second day in a row, after Moscow launched strikes on Kyiv’s bridges. Crimea’s Moscow-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces had struck the bridge and traffic had been suspended. On Monday, a Ukrainian drone crashed into one of the Kerch bridge’s arches . Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up. Russian strikes hit two major bridges in Kyiv late on Monday, part of an overnight attack that damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted heating and water in parts of the Ukrainian capital, its mayor said. The North and South bridges were hit, Vitali Klitschko said, citing preliminary information, in a post on Telegram just before midnight local time (2200 GMT), shortly after the Ukrainian air force warned of incoming missiles. He later said critical infrastructure systems were damaged and that heating and water supplies in some districts were affected. Air defence units were in operation in the city, he said, while witnesses ‌reported a series of loud explosions. articles.title: Meet Will Lawrence: Sunrise Movement Co-Founder Elected to Congress on Anti-Data Center Platform
articles.description: Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech. “I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’” Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.

articles.title: "We Have to Be Brave": Palestinian Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh Speaks Out After Israeli Detention
articles.description: The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara. “Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

articles.title: Pentagon Whistleblower Wes Bryant: Impeach Hegseth. He's a "Clear & Present Danger" to Democracy
articles.description: The House of Representatives is moving toward a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. They include violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran after Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop, illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” by bombing the boats of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, abducting President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for his participation in a video reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. If the House votes for impeachment, it will prompt a Senate trial that could end with removal from office. “Under Hegseth, the U.S. military has been hijacked,” says retired Air Force Master Sergeant Wes Bryant, who served as chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from 2024 to 2025. “America has portrayed itself to the world as a far-right dictatorship bent on global domination, and Hegseth and his wielding of the U.S. military with free rein from Donald Trump is really the primary enforcer of that.” Bryant adds that “Hegseth should be the first domino,” but that Trump, as well as “many of our senior military leaders,” should also be impeached.

articles.title: Latino Voters Swing Away from Trump for "Terrorizing Our Communities": Marisa Franco of Mijente
articles.description: In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump. We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. While ICE brutality will be at the front of voters’ minds, she says, Democrats cannot continue to take Latino voters for granted. “The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation,” explains Franco. “And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control. So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them.”

articles.title: Election Protection: NAACP on Voter Suppression & Deployment of Federal Poll Monitors
articles.description: As President Donald Trump continues to cast doubt on the integrity of U.S. elections, signaling his intentions to challenge results unfavorable to Republicans, we go to Washington, D.C., where a federal judge ruled Monday night that the Department of Justice can deploy election monitors to polling sites across the country, as long as they are not law enforcement officers with the power to make arrests. “In some respects, this is a victory for voters. Every voter in our country deserves to be able to cast a ballot today, free from intimidation,” says Kristen Clarke of the NAACP , which sued to challenge the DOJ’s plans to deploy ICE agents and other armed officers to the polls. The NAACP was also part of a coalition that intervened when the Trump administration attempted to force California to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleged were sent incorrectly to noncitizens. “This was a baseless, error-prone, shoddy 11th-hour attempt to hijack the election in California, plain and simple, and it’s now been rejected by four courts,” Clarke says. The administration’s attacks on voters “are not bearing fruit,” she adds. “We anticipate and are ready for anything that they may throw our way.”

Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. articles.title: From Ranked-Choice Voting to Dumping Electoral College: Rob Richie on Election Reform Movement
articles.description: Alaska is the only Senate race yet to be called. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with about 86% of votes counted. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, a system where voters choose not only their top candidate, but can also indicate an order of preference for remaining candidates on the ballot. If no candidate wins a majority as the top choice, then second-choice votes are added to the totals and so on until there is a winner. Rob Richie, president and founder of Expand Democracy and a senior adviser with FairVote, explains how ranked-choice voting has shaped the Alaska race and how it is “a system that promotes [candidates] reaching out, engaging, and, for voters, a lot of freedom.” Richie adds that Peltola is “heavily favored to win at this point.”

articles.title: Relatives of Slain Freedom Summer Activists Celebrate Scott Colom's Historic Senate Win in Mississippi
articles.description: Democrat Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The electoral breakthrough is particularly meaningful given Mississippi’s history in the civil rights movement. In 1964, three civil rights activists — James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman — were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan after traveling to the state to register Black voters. We speak with two of their relatives about Colom’s stunning upset. “I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed,” says Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney. “The people of Mississippi have spoken,” adds David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. “And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America.”

articles.title: Scott Colom Wins Stunning Victory, Becomes Mississippi's First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
articles.description: Democrat Scott Colom has made history as Mississippi’s first Democratic senator since 1982 — and its first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that President Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Colom’s victory brings the incoming Senate Democratic caucus to 55. Colom gave his victory speech on Wednesday at the historically Black Tougaloo College, just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan. “There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith,” said Colom. “There are so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible, people like Medgar Evers.”

articles.title: "They Have Eyes": How Trump's Corruption Became a Top Concern for Midterm Voters
articles.description: Democrats regained control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday’s historic midterm elections, a comeback fueled largely by voter anger over high prices and the war on Iran. But surveys also found that corruption was a major concern, with 76% of voters telling a Harris poll that elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 63% of Americans considered it inappropriate for Trump and his family to profit from cryptocurrency, while 69% said his private business interests influence his decisions as president. “If this election was about corruption and cost, then this next Congress needs to be focused on accountability and affordability,” says Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW . “Congress needs to do oversight not just on the administration’s corruption, not just on the president’s profiteering, but also on corporate America, what they have gotten out of engaging in the president’s pay-to-play environment, how corporate America and the outside influence of money in our political system has undermined the public voice in our policy discussions.”

articles.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
articles.description: Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too. Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. articles.description: Andreeva seals 7-5, 6-3 victory to earn world No 2 ranking Russian dominates tournament without losing a set Mirra Andreeva had put herself on the brink of securing another effortless, straightforward set in one of the biggest finals of her career when she momentarily balked. Serving for the first set at 5-4, Andreeva nervously opened the game with two dire double faults before spraying two further unforced errors to hand over the break. There have already been many times in Andreeva’s young career when similar sequences triggered epic, dramatic collapses, so prone the 19-year-old has been to losing her composure when things do not go her way. This time, she betrayed no negative emotions at all. articles.title: Electric vehicle targets and reality are now on a collision course | Letters
articles.description: Paul English says the cheap home charging that makes EVs economical is out of reach for many, while Mike Hawes wonders if consumers are ready to switch. Plus letters from Ben Plowden and Anne Maclennan George Monbiot is right that European carmakers have dragged their feet, but his column describes only half the problem ( Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? articles.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
articles.description: Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations Your article ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century. There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
articles.description: Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
articles.description: Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “ reactive and risk-averse ” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?” This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “ human bandwidth ”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage. articles.title: Spark review – Glyndebourne Youth Opera light up a terrific new show of monsters and magic
articles.description: Glyndebourne, Lewes Lucy Armstrong’s family opera transports audiences to a secret world above the rooftops. It explores themes of grief and loss with a lightness of touch, and is directed, designed and performed with panache. For decades now, Glyndebourne has been setting the bar for what a youth opera company can be. Its latest show is Spark, a new full-length opera directed by Fiona Dunn with music by Lucy Armstrong, exploring grownup themes of grief and loss. Spark is a story of a parallel world accessed via something unlikely, so there are shades of Narnia or Wonderland. Our heroine is Clara (shades of The Nutcracker), who has panic attacks when she tries to go to school: “They talk like it’s simple,” she says in Olivia Bell’s succinct, fluent libretto, “but my chest is tightening and I can’t breathe.” We find out that her anxiety stems from her grief for her brother, and that she can no longer connect with her parents, who are having connection problems of their own. But she can escape up the chimney to a rooftop land populated by Spark Monsters – who will help her regain her lost spark, pun intended. Continue reading...
