articles.title: Gen X is in worse health than boomers – and I have a few theories as to why | Emma Beddington
articles.description: People in my age group are experiencing poorer physical and mental health than their elders at the same stage. Is this down to UPFs and booze, or something more complicated? I almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies , on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”. Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (unsure). articles.description: Slow-cooked pork in a deliciously sweet-salty glaze is Vietnamese comfort food at its best Many moons ago, I attended a cookery class in Hanoi that revealed to me the glories of thịt kho tàu , a simple but unbelievably delicious dish of caramelised pork braised in sweet coconut water and savoury fish sauce, enlivened by plenty of black pepper. In fact, loved it so much that I put their version in my cookbook, The A to Z of Eating, and then somehow forgot all about it for a decade. It’s easy to do that when you’re always working on the next recipe, but this week has been a very welcome rediscovery, not least because I’ve learned a lot more about what chef Thuy Diem Pham describes in her book The Little Viet Kitchen as “the ultimate home comfort food”. articles.description: Whether you want minimalist or heritage, waterproof or suede, our menswear expert has rounded up the most stylish pairs for every occasion and outfit • The best men’s coats for autumn and winter I haven’t always worn boots. For years I wrote them off – at 5ft 8in, I was convinced anything above the ankle would make my legs look shorter. Then I started wearing them with the right trousers – a straight leg that falls over the top – and realised I’d spent a decade getting winter wrong. articles.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
articles.description: From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out? In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most. The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line , in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.” In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn , announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social homes target of 60%. articles.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
articles.description: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...

articles.description: In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage . When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan. articles.title: Blacklock, Birmingham B3: ‘A very, very cool version of an Angus Steakhouse’ – restaurant review
articles.description: Ever-open, eminently relatable, sensibly priced spots of this sort will always have an audience A London chophouse has taken up residence on St Philip’s Place, Birmingham, on the edge of Cathedral Square, or “Pigeon Park”, as the locals call it. This particular nook of Brum city centre is a magnet to those feathered blighters, although Blacklock ’s smoulderingly macho menu is ironically pigeon-meat free, revolving instead around heaps of chops and steaks cooked over charcoal. There’s porterhouse, bone-in sirloin, lamb rump and pig’s head on toast. Launched in London in 2015 , Blacklock was the elegant, edgy, no-nonsense dining experience for groovy young things who quite literally wanted meat and two veg, so long as said veg was dripping-fat chips; it now has five sites in the capital and another in Manchester. “We just ended up at Blacklock,” people used to tell me half a dozen times a week, then go on to rave about the bread, the gravy and the ash-baked sweet potatoes, and revel in the glorious simplicity of it all. Modern life was complex, Blacklock was not, but neither was it cheap enough to feel like a jaunt down the Toby Carvery . And now its big flavours and broad appeal have hit the UK’s second city. For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. articles.title: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
articles.description: As teenagers, my friends and I thought it was glamorous to have relationships with older men. But after the revelations about Russell Brand and David Walliams, I have started to see that period of my life in a new light It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us . Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé . We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience. A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. I would have thought consent would be taken as a blanket statement that covered whatever followed, however horrifying and unwanted; that I’d made my bed, so was obliged to lie in it, come what may. My friends, it should be noted, felt the same. Thank God the heroic woman forced to endure Brand’s attack knew better. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: Honey review – a hugely entertaining Killing Eve prequel that’s packed with naughty jokes
articles.description: This tale of a young female spy in 1980s East Berlin is a visual delight. Around every corner is a fun comic twist Is there any more alluring aesthetic in screen fiction than the iron curtain thriller? Any TV show dealing in 1980s cold war chic – Deutschland 83, Kleo, Star City, The Same Sky, the Russian bits of The Americans – probably has an irresistible mix of danger, absurdity and exotic kitsch. Moustaches! Wigs! Leather trench coats! Rigid patterned fabrics! Cassette players! Boxy cars! The chilly ennui of oppressed citizens and the flagrant risk-taking of secret agents, all somehow liberated by an existential inner emptiness! It’s just so much fun. Honey pitches us straight into premium frosty paranoia with an opening scene in which British “press attache” – ie spy handler – Graham Anderson (Rory Kinnear, hoorah!) endures a nervous crossing back into East Berlin, during which he really, really does not want his car to be searched. The crowning indignity of his interaction with a chortling buffoon of a border guard is when the manchild in uniform eyeballs Graham’s wife, Anne (Sonita Henry – a slightly more niche hoorah if you saw her fine turns in Silo or The Chelsea Detective), in the passenger seat and decides to show off how closely the pair are being surveilled: “Good luck for your smear test on Thursday, Mrs Anderson!” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘All I could smell was fertiliser’: the best (and worst) supermarket instant coffee, tasted and rated
articles.description: Our coffee snob spills the beans on which granules hint at chocolate and caramel, and which leave a bitter note • Everything you need to make great coffee I’m a coffee snob with my own grinder, but I found the haptic thwack, whack and crack of opening the lid and film on a jar of instant coffee strangely invigorating, and rather nostalgic. When I took a deep sniff, however, disaster: all I could smell was fertiliser! Instant coffee is brewed at scorching temperatures, then either freeze-dried in a vacuum or spray-dried using hot air. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. This gives it an earthier, muskier and more bitter flavour profile, though, thankfully, with a little alchemy and hot water, those more familiar coffee aromas and flavours returned, with notes of chicory, bitter chocolate and burnt sugar. Almost all of these products have a similar industrial imprint, uniform granules and a one-dimensional flavour profile, so they’re ultimately more a simulation of the real thing. That said, some did surprise me. At best, they taste like a cup of office filter coffee, made in a commercial drip machine and left just long enough for its aromas to fade. At worst, instant coffee tastes like cardboard and burnt rubber steeped in water. The addition of milk, however, transforms many cups and makes them far more drinkable and even comforting, bringing out notes of chocolate, nuts and caramel. Continue reading...

She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. articles.title: ‘Seduced by a dramatic landscape of canyons and lakes’: exploring Catalonia’s wild side
articles.description: A historic single-track train line through the foothills of the Pyrenees opens up a pristine wilderness of forests, gorges and thundering rivers Alighting at the train station of Santa Linya in northern Spain, I paused to wonder what the railway engineers were thinking. A rough halt hewn out of the mountainside, with no ticket office, no waiting room, no sign of human habitation – just a single platform in the wilderness. On the far side of the track, a shimmering turquoise lake flanked by pine forests. Ahead – the only way out – a rocky trail snaking up the limestone cliff. My husband and I had first strayed into this western corner of Catalonia – Pallars Jussà – on our honeymoon road trip 21 years earlier. Seduced by its dramatic landscape of canyons, lakes, crumbling ruins and the formidable Noguera Pallaresa river thundering south from the Pyrenees, we had vowed to return one day. He loves mountains, I love water, we both love abandoned buildings; it was a geographical match made in heaven. Now those vows had come good – we were back, on a mission to go deeper into the hinterland. Continue reading...

articles.description: All of Hollywood’s biggest stars are in attendance for the Governors’ awards, but nobody gets drunk and the biggest draw is an awkward documentarian Timothée Chalamet was seconds away from getting into trouble. It was just after 6pm in Hollywood and Lynette Howell Taylor, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, was trying to corral a crowd of 700-odd people into sitting down so she could begin the Governors awards ceremony. She jokingly threatened to start calling out anyone still standing by name if they didn’t sit down imminently. Chalamet was the only one left on his feet, circling the table where he was due to sit next to his girlfriend, Kylie Jenner, opposite Tom Holland and Zendaya. Howell Taylor gave him a few seconds’ grace. He looked like the popular kid testing how far he could push a headteacher. The Governors awards had a curiously school-like atmosphere this year. Even the carpet in the Ray Dolby Ballroom was faded and striped. The social structure was much the same: closed-off and insular, with cliques, alliances, legendary enmities and intricate hierarchies of popularity and influence. There were those who seemed entirely comfortable – Chalamet, Holland, Tom Cruise, Matt Damon, Willem Dafoe, Seth Rogen – and others still angling for a better table. Continue reading...

articles.description: Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “ welcome back ” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “ Breturn ” has yet to catch on. By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to avoid pre-empting the broader “conversation” that he desires on relations with the EU. articles.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
articles.description: From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “ war minus the shooting ”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday? Even those who don’t understand the finer points of the rolling maul can surely grasp why this result matters. For much of the last century, heavy industry and rugby were twin pillars of Welsh national identity. The heavy industry is largely gone, and over the past few years, rugby has looked to be going the same way: a weakened national team; financial problems that threatened to tear apart the domestic rugby set-up in Wales; and the growing appeal of football . Until Saturday, Welsh sports fans looking for a winning finish were better off watching the darts champion Gerwyn “The Iceman” Price than Steve Tandy’s rugby team . articles.description: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. articles.title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old. There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service , careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation , scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold , the leisure centres closed , the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back . That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. Let that begin here. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.description: The foreign secretary played his cards carefully as the PM prepared to tell us he wants a reset with Europe So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Brexit is the wound that will never heal, despite the ministrations of countless Grail knights. More than 10 years have passed and still our politics is defined by the sliding doors moment of the EU referendum. Everything dragging us back to that June day in 2016. The further we get from it, the closer it becomes. Something only Stephen Hawking could have explained. And then, only to himself. The rest of us would have been none the wiser. For the most part, we’ve tried to avoid talking about the subject. At least in public. It’s considered impolite, an intrusion into a national grief. In private, most people now admit the country is worse off than we were before we left the EU. But it is a pain and misfortune that must be borne stoically. The people had spoken. And the people can never be wrong. Except when they are. The Guardian’s year in review 2026 . articles.description: Grand Palais, Paris The fair celebrated the bicentenary of photography – but did anyone care? Especially when the most compelling images proposed whole new ways of seeing No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist. This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human? | Zoe Williams
articles.description: The understanding of refugees as complex individuals, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs, often seems to have been lost. A new film offers a different, truer, perspective There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing. There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a diaspora talking about their parents. There are refugees en masse, shorn of any traits or qualities at all, discussed purely in terms of whether or not the host state can accommodate them, and how long they should be allowed to stay in any given place.
